1:
Keil and Delitzsch open with the plan of the chapter: after prophesying generally of the judgment coming on both kingdoms for apostasy, the prophet turns here to what he treats as the principal sins, the injustice and oppression practised by the great, for which the nation was to be driven from its inheritance; then he vindicates that threat against the false prophets who confirmed the people in ungodliness by their lies. Clarke gives the same sequence with an added observation about the manner of it, that an Israelite is introduced part way through as a mourner, personating his people and lamenting their fate. Henry names the ground of the controversy in one word, oppression, which he says is as often mentioned as any sin in hastening the ruin of nations and families, and then sets out its steps in order.

The first step, on Henry's reckoning, is the eager desire of what is not one's own, which he calls the root of bitterness and the root of all evil; and he puts the covetous reasoning into the mouth of the offender, that such a man's field and house lie convenient for me, that they are fitter for me than for him, and that I would manage them better than he does. The second step is the setting of the wits to work, devising the thing with a great deal of cursed art and policy so as to accomplish it effectually and yet without exposing oneself to danger or reproach. Ellicott finds the same deliberateness in the wording rather than the psychology, noting a gradation in the terms which marks the acts as considered and unextenuated: the plan is formed in the night, thought out upon the bed, and carried into execution in the morning; and he compares the gradation of walking, standing and sitting by which the first psalm describes a deepening intercourse with the wicked.

Gill takes the word rendered iniquity as broad enough to cover several sins at once. It is sometimes used for an idol, so idolatry may be meant; or the sin of uncleanness, on which thoughts too often dwell in the night season; or the coveting of a neighbour's goods and the oppression of the poor. Wesley reduces the verse to three glosses, that they contrive and frame mischief, that they contrive how to work it, and that the reason given for their confidence is simply that they can, without regarding right or wrong.

Three of them reach for the same precedent when the coveting turns to seizure. Gill has the offenders wishing their poor neighbours' fields were theirs, contriving to obtain them, and if fair means fail either using some crafty method or taking them by force, as Ahab got Naboth's vineyard; Clarke names the same case and says these rich and mighty men will take the inheritance of any poor Naboth on whom their covetous eye may fix. Ellicott presses the point further, that the seizure of that vineyard by violence and murder was no isolated incident but an instance of a settled appetite for accumulating land in contravention of the law, an appetite denounced in the same generation by the prophet who cried woe on those who join house to house and lay field to field till there is no place left. Calvin fixes on the speed of it: as soon as they have coveted anything they take it by force, so that the previous verse's wicked counsels are joined to the attempt at effecting them, the men being as bold and daring in execution as they were skilful in contrivance. Wesley adds the legal aggravation, that this was done against ancient right and possession in a case where God had forbidden the owner to sell his heritage at all.
3:
The sentence is read by all of them as an exact retaliation, and three say so in almost the same words. Ellicott puts it that as they devise evil against their brethren, so God is devising an evil against them, and that they shall bow their necks under a hostile yoke. Wesley makes the same correspondence and extends it to the posture: God will devise evil against their family as they devised it against the family of their neighbours, and having made others hang the head they shall now hang their own. Clarke states the exchange plainly — you have devised the evil of plundering the upright, and I will devise the evil of punishment for your conduct — and then names the historical instrument, the Assyrian king who ruined the kingdom and transported the people. Calvin adds the reason the threat was needed: the avaricious were elevated in vain by their frauds and rapacity, since their hope would be disappointed and God was waiting in heaven for his time to appear against them. He also weighs the word rendered family, which he takes to designate the people of Israel. Gill identifies the family with the whole nation and the ten tribes in particular, among whom these sins chiefly prevailed.

Who is heard taking up the lamentation divides them four ways. Ellicott makes it the enemy, who will repeat in mockery the doleful lamentations with which the sufferers bewail their own pitiable state. Gill reports two possibilities and prefers the second, that a false prophet speaks, finding his promises come to nothing, or rather that a stranger and bystander does, a mere spectator of their miseries; he also allows the phrase to mean concerning you rather than against you, so that what follows is a narrative of their troubles delivered in figurative terms. Wesley divides the mourning between two parties, their friends lamenting for them and they for themselves. Clarke treats the whole as a funeral dirge composed and sung for them as for the dead, and marks where it begins and ends.

One clause in the lament is construed two quite different ways. Ellicott renders it that God has divided their fields to an apostate, meaning an idolater, so that the land these men were taking from others would be handed over to an idolatrous king. Wesley takes the same words adverbially of God rather than of a recipient, that turning away from them in displeasure he has divided their fields among others. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as turning away he has divided our fields, leaving the ambiguity standing in their text.

The loss of the measuring line is the sharpest image of the passage, and Calvin explains why it bites. The land had been given to the posterity of Abraham on the condition of being held as a heritage, and a line was determined by lot whenever the year of jubilee returned, so that every man might regain his own possession; the threat is therefore that God would cleanse the country of its perverse inhabitants so that it should no longer be the inheritance of that people. Clarke says the same more briefly, that the inheritance will no more be divided to them by lot as it was to their fathers and they shall have neither fields nor possessions of any kind. Ellicott takes the loss to be of any part or inheritance in the congregation at all, and Wesley presses it furthest, that none shall ever return to see the land allotted by line, and that they shall no more be the congregation of the Lord, nor their children after them. Gill leaves the person addressed open between the false prophet, the oppressors, and the whole people, inclining to the last.
6:
Two of them begin by admitting that the verse is hard. Ellicott says its construction is very confused while its intention is fairly clear, and states that intention as an exchange: it contains the address of the oppressors to the true prophets, and the prophets' reply. Calvin says the conciseness of the expressions has made interpreters differ, and sets out the reading he thinks best, that the Jews are speaking against the prophets and forbidding them with threats, as though with authority. On that reading he finds the arrogance the more remarkable, since ungodly men who wish to take away the liberty of teaching from God's prophets resist them as though they were themselves doubly and trebly prophets.

The verb at the centre of the dispute is glossed by four of them in the same direction. Calvin observes that the Hebrew word for distilling means the same as to speak, though it is applied more commonly to weighty addresses than to common and ordinary ones. Clarke renders it literally as a prohibition against causing it to rain, and notes that raining often stands for preaching or prophesying in several other prophets and in the wisdom books. Keil and Delitzsch render it drip not, glossing it at once as prophesy not, and keep the same word for the reply. Gill takes the image as one of profusion, that such terrible words are not to flow from the prophets' lips in such abundance, and that they are to cease speaking in the name of the Lord if nothing can be heard from them but sharp reproofs and severe judgments.

Gill also reports a construction none of the others adopts. On this reading the first word forbids the true prophets while the second should be rendered as a permission — let them prophesy — and applied to the false prophets who prophesy smooth things, so that the whole sentence means let the one speak but not the other. Henry states what makes the prohibition so grave: to persecute and silence prophets provokes God as much as anything, since it not only spits in the face of his authority over us but spurns at the bowels of his mercy to us, the sending of prophets being a sure and valuable token of his goodwill; and he pairs this sin with the oppression of the poor as the two charges of the chapter, each answered by a judgment that exactly matches it.

The closing clause is taken two ways, and the question is whose shame is meant. Clarke reports a rendering that makes it the prophet's own, that he shall not remove reproaches from himself, and passes on the paraphrase that a true prophet will subject himself to public disgrace by the mere exercise of his office. Wesley and Ellicott both put the shame on the hearers instead: Wesley glosses the phrase as describing those who will not take shame to themselves, and adds a grim observation on the sentence that they shall not prophesy, that God in his displeasure grants the people their own request; Ellicott has the prophesying continue but without benefit to those who will not put their shame away. Keil and Delitzsch supply the context of the refusal, that the people are abusing the long-suffering and mercy of the Lord, and that by robbing the peaceable poor and the widows and the fatherless they are bringing on themselves the punishment of banishment out of the land.
7:
Who asks whether the Spirit is straitened is genuinely disputed. Clarke makes the question the people's, a piece of their own complaint continuing the lamentation, so that they are asking whether the Spirit still speaks by others as it did formerly and whether these evils are really his doing; and on that reading the answer comes from God in the clause that follows, that no upright man need fear any word spoken by him. Ellicott reverses the direction and has the prophet expostulating with a people who are the Lord's in name only, the Spirit who does not change being still the same toward them while they brought their sufferings on themselves. Wesley divides the verse between the two, taking the first question as the assertion that God's power and wisdom and kindness are not less now than formerly, and the second as the people's protest whether such severe proceedings are what their God delights in.

Calvin takes the whole as a rebuke of presumption and states it sharply. The people were inflated enough to wish to make terms with God, saying let him not prophesy as though it were in man's power to rule God; and since the prophets did not speak of themselves but by command, being the organs of the Holy Spirit, to attempt to silence them is to try to subject the Spirit of God to one's own pleasure. Gill and Wesley both fasten on the title given them, that they are called the house of Jacob after a great and good man and are reckoned religious people, but have the name only and not the thing, being the degenerate offspring of that patriarch.

Against whom the people have risen as an enemy is answered four ways. Gill takes it of their brethren, not only of God and true religion through idolatry, and points to the slaughter in the days of a king of Israel when a hundred and twenty thousand of Judah fell. Wesley multiplies the fractures — Israel against Judah and Judah against Israel, the tribes conspiring against one another, subjects against their kings, and the great ones against the meaner sort. Clarke generalises it to mutual enmity, that they are not only opposed to God but enemies to each other, robbing and spoiling one another. Ellicott narrows it instead to a particular crime, the continued rapacity that stripped the quiet inoffensive traveller of both his outer and his inner garment, taking away cloak and coat together as the gospel saying has it.

Calvin, before offering any of this, warns that the verse will not yield a single certain sense. The prophet's words are concise, he says, and therefore contain some obscurity, so that interpreters differ; and he works through the disputed opening word, reporting the division over whether it is one word or two and settling for the ordinary meaning of yesterday, with the caution that the Hebrews do not use yesterday strictly but let it stand for past time even when many years have gone by. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause in that key, that but yesterday the people rise up as an enemy and draw the cloak off from the garment of those who pass by carelessly and averted from war.
9:
The wrong done to the women is described with a common indignation and a difference of detail. Gill has the offenders not content with slaying the husbands but taking the wives and widows captive and dispossessing them of habitations where they had lived delightfully with husbands and children, and he supplies the instance of two hundred thousand of their brethren's women carried off to Samaria. Clarke lays the whole train of consequences at their door, that they are the cause of women and children being carried into captivity, separated from their pleasant habitations and from the temple and its ordinances and from the blessings of the covenant — which, he says, it is God's glory to give and theirs to receive. Wesley presses the legal point, that the children were turned out of houses and estates which the law secured from any sale beyond the jubilee, and that these men had nevertheless confiscated them for ever. Ellicott states it in a line, that they spared not even the widows and the fatherless, who are the objects of God's tender care.

Calvin explains what makes the following sentence so heavy. The land had been honoured by God with the distinction of being a rest, and not merely the people's rest but his own, as the oath declares that they should not enter into my rest; so it was a rest hidden under the wings of God, assigned as an inheritance to a chosen people among whom he himself dwelt. Ellicott turns the same clause into requital, that the Lord, repaying them for their cruelty to the poor and defenceless, declares their own time of trouble imminent and the polluted land no place of rest for them. Wesley adds the condition on which the rest had been given, continued obedience, and says the land will spue them out.

Whom the command to arise and depart addresses is not agreed. Gill and Wesley take it as spoken to the offenders and the people at large, a summons to prepare for captivity and exile and to expect at any moment to be told to be gone, since men who drove others from their inheritances shall have this for their own case. Clarke gives the same sense first and then reports another: some think the words are an exhortation to the godly, telling them to leave a land that was so soon to be destroyed. Keil and Delitzsch simply render the sentence as the banishment which such conduct must be followed by.

On the false prophet the voices converge and then each adds something. Gill reports the marginal rendering that the man walks with the wind and lies falsely, being full of wind and vanity and following the dictates of his own spirit. Ellicott calls it a lying spirit speaking the smooth and pleasant things the people loved, after the fashion of the court prophet who struck the true one on the cheek, and quotes another prophet's complaint that the prophets prophesy falsely and the people love to have it so. Calvin identifies the disease as the wish to be soothed with flatteries, since the ungodly reckon themselves in a manner exempt from God's judgment when they hear no reproof and count themselves happy when they find flatterers indulgent to their vices; he mentions that an earlier commentator sought a quite different meaning here, as in the previous verses, and declines to stop and refute him. Clarke draws the application into his own century, observing how often the worldling who has entered the priest's office for a maintenance, and leaves people undisturbed in an unregenerate state, is the better received of the two.
12:
Almost everyone reads the closing two verses as the promise that conventionally ends such a chapter, and Calvin alone does not. Henry states the convention as such, that after threatenings of wrath a prophecy usually concludes with promises of mercy, and takes these as fulfilled in part when the Jews returned from Babylon and fully in the kingdom of the Messiah, so that the dispersed are brought together again with not one lost or missing, the remnant designed and reserved for salvation being gathered. Clarke calls it plainly a promise of restoration from captivity. Wesley divides the fulfilment the same way as Henry, partly at the return from Babylon and more fully when Christ by his gospel gathered into one all the scattered children of God. Gill reports a different possibility before adopting one, that the words may be the false prophet's own continued, promising plenty and prosperity and the return of the captive tribes to live together in safety.

Calvin says outright that the exposition of the passage is twofold and that he is going against the current. The greater part of interpreters, he grants, take it that God promises some alleviation after having sharply reproved the people and threatened utter ruin, and they apply the passage accordingly to the kingdom of Christ as giving hope of a future restoration. But when he weighs everything narrowly he finds himself forced to the contrary view, that these two verses are a commination in which the prophet denounces God's future vengeance; and he acknowledges that the other opinion is almost universally received before setting out his own.

On that reading the details change their sense entirely. Where the others hear a fold, Calvin hears a rout: the people shall be led away in confusion, and the gate shall be broken so that they may go forth together, since the passage would not be wide enough if they went out in regular order as men usually do, and the gates of cities must be broken that they may pass through in great numbers and in disorder. The whole, he says, intimates that all would quickly be taken into exile; and the king who goes before them is, on his account, a king made captive, which he calls the saddest spectacle of all, since some hope remained while only the dregs of the people had been carried off.

Clarke reads the same images the other way and fills them out. The noise of the assembled flock he explains from the animals themselves, since when a hundred sheep run together the eight hundred divisions of their cloven hoofs make a wonderful clattering, and he takes that for the image intended. The breaker is for him the one who gives deliverance and leads them out on the way of their return, taking down the hurdles or making a gap in the wall to let them through, which he applies to whatever human agents should order the return, while the Lord going at their head he refers to a final restoration under Christ as their leader. Wesley hovers between the two readings, glossing the gate as the door of escape out of captivity and at the same time observing that no city is so strong that the Assyrians shall not take it and enter in through its gates, and he compares the Lord at their head to his going before Israel out of Egypt. Gill lists and rejects several identifications of the breaker — the enemy army breaking down a city wall, the king who escaped through such a breach, and the Maccabees who delivered the Jews afterwards — before settling on his own. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse without interpretation, the breaker gone up before them, the gate passed through, and their king going before them with the Lord at their head.
